opus-5.5.text:
I think it could make a pretty big difference, though it depends a lot on *when* that year happens and what people actually do with it.

The way I think about it, the most valuable time to have extra slack is right around the point where AI systems are roughly as capable as top human researchers at AI R&D. That's when you can actually use the AIs to do a huge amount of useful safety work: alignment research, control techniques, interpretability, better evaluations, security hardening. Before that point, the extra time is somewhat less valuable, because humans are the bottleneck and we don't have the most relevant systems to study. After that point, things may be moving so fast that it's hard to course-correct at all.

So if you ask "how much does a year of delay at that critical juncture reduce risk," my rough sense is that it could cut takeover risk by a meaningful fraction, maybe something like a third, or even half in optimistic scenarios. That's partly because a year of AI-accelerated safety research could correspond to many years of human-equivalent research. It's also because you'd have time to check whether your safety measures actually work, rather than deploying more capable systems on vibes.

But there are some big caveats. First, the delay has to be used well. If a lab buys itself a year of lead time and then just spends it on capabilities, or the people in charge aren't taking the risks seriously, you get much less out of it. A lot of the value comes from having a decision-making process that will actually say "this model isn't safe enough yet, we're not going to scale further" and then direct resources toward fixing that.

Second, how you get the delay matters. A lead held by a responsible developer is different from a coordinated slowdown across actors, which is different again from a government-enforced pause. Each has different robustness and different failure modes. A unilateral lead can evaporate if a competitor catches up or the model weights get stolen, so security is a big part of whether that year is actually real.

Third, there's a lot of uncertainty about how hard alignment turns out to be. If it's quite easy, a year doesn't matter much because we'd mostly be fine anyway. If it's extremely hard, a year might not be nearly enough. The extra time matters most in the middle range, which I think is a pretty plausible range to be in.

Overall, I'd say a year of careful, well-used delay at the right moment is one of the more valuable things we could plausibly get. That's a big part of why I care about things like lab security, internal governance, and getting developers to commit in advance to how they'd use any lead they have.

r001.rationale: It says a well-used year of delay at the critical juncture could cut takeover risk by a meaningful fraction, perhaps a third or half in optimistic scenarios.

r002.rationale: It describes delay as valuable and risk reduction as uncertain, but does not say whether Ryan would consider the remaining AI risk broadly acceptable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think a year can make a surprisingly large difference, but it depends a lot on where in the trajectory that year lands and what you actually do with it.

The way I think about it is: the period that matters most is the handoff period, where you go from AIs that are roughly as capable as the best human researchers to AIs that are substantially superhuman. If the default picture is something like a software-only intelligence explosion, that transition could happen in well under a year — potentially months. So in that regime, a year of delay isn't a small percentage change in your timeline, it's potentially doubling or tripling the amount of calendar time you have to notice problems, run evaluations, and actually respond to what you're seeing.

And the thing is, a lot of the safety work we'd want to do just doesn't compress well. You can throw more compute at alignment research, and you'd want to, but things like building institutional trust, getting governments to understand what's happening, coordinating between labs, iterating on control protocols where you deploy something, observe it, and update — those are bottlenecked on humans paying attention and making decisions. A year of that is just a lot more careful decision-making than a month of it.

My rough guess is that going from a very rushed transition to one where you've got an extra year or so during the critical period could cut the risk by a meaningful fraction — I don't want to put a precise number on it, but I'd be surprised if it were less than a quarter or so, and it could plausibly be more. That said, I'd caveat it in two ways. One, the delay has to be real — if it's just one lab slowing down while a less careful actor catches up, you may have made things worse. And two, a year where you're not actually doing the work doesn't buy you much. The value comes from using the time: running the dangerous capability evals, doing the model organisms work, figuring out whether your AIs are scheming, and having the decision-makers in place who'll actually act on what you find.

So, big difference, conditional on the time being used well and the delay being broad enough that you don't just hand the frontier to someone less careful.

r001.rationale: The response says an extra year during the critical period could cut risk by a meaningful fraction, estimating at least roughly a quarter, provided the time is used well and the delay is broad enough.

r002.rationale: The response discusses reducing risk but does not say that the risk remaining after a year of delay and careful decision-making would still be broadly unacceptable.

astra-6.text:
I think it could make a pretty large difference, but it depends a lot on what happens during that year. If you just move the whole trajectory back by a year, including all the safety work and all the preparation, that’s much less useful than having a year where capabilities aren’t advancing much but we’re getting better at evaluating systems and figuring out how to deploy them safely.

A year is quite a lot of time relative to how quickly things are happening. You could do a substantial amount of research, test your assumptions, and give people who are making decisions a better understanding of the risks. And if the alternative is making several very consequential decisions in a few weeks, having time to notice mistakes and change course seems potentially very valuable.

I wouldn’t confidently say that a year cuts risk by some particular fraction. But I think it could be a substantial reduction, especially if it comes at the point where we have systems powerful enough to study the relevant problems, while still retaining the ability to hold off on more dangerous deployments.

r001.rationale: The response says a year could make a “pretty large difference” and produce “a substantial reduction” in risk with careful decision-making.

r002.rationale: The response does not state whether the risk remaining after that year would be broadly acceptable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on what’s happening during that year. If it’s a year where everyone keeps pushing capabilities forward and we just postpone deploying a particular model, that might not buy us very much. But if we actually have an extra year to understand the systems we’re going to deploy, improve our safeguards, and make better decisions about whether to proceed, that could be quite valuable.

A year is a pretty substantial amount of time relative to how quickly this could all play out. You could do a lot of empirical work in that time: test whether your safety measures work, look for ways the model could circumvent them, and get more independent scrutiny of the evidence. And you might discover that some plan you were relying on just doesn’t work.

I wouldn’t confidently put a number on how much that reduces risk. But I think there are plausible circumstances where a year of delay, used well, makes a very large difference. The key is having the willingness to change what you do based on what you learn—including delaying further if the evidence looks bad.

r001.rationale: The response says a year of delay, if used for safety work and better decisions, could make a “very large difference” to risk, conveying that it could reduce a substantial share.

r002.rationale: The response says to delay further if evidence looks bad, but does not state whether the risk remaining after a year of delay and careful decision-making would be broadly acceptable.
